item.title: Model Pluralism
item.description:
This is a crosspost from my Substack.

I suspect that most of the readers of this newsletter haven’t read much or any literature in the philosophy of science. But it’s an exciting field. After all, how does science work and why is it our best guide to reality? Some of the most puzzling questions in the philosophy of science concern what models are, how they work, and how we can make sense of the plurality of models.

Most people think that a diversity of models is a bad thing, a sign of an immature science, and that future science will reduce all of these models to something like a single master model. I think that’s a mistake and model pluralism should be embraced. If you’re interested in learning a bit more about scientific modelling, read on.

1. Introduction

In this essay (pdf copy here), I introduce an account of models, modeling, and model-based science (abbreviated henceforth as MMM) that I dub model pluralism. Accordingly, the title of this paper is intended to reflect the incredible diversity of models, their purposes and roles in science—components of MMM, that though starting to become more and more recognized, undermine an essential tenet of the literature at large.

In the face of the incredible diversity of both models and modeling practices, a naive form of model monism appears untenable. Mitchell calls pluralism in science simply a “fact,” which is no overstatement.¹

However, there is a certain ambiguity in how model pluralism might be understood: is it (i) merely a descriptive claim, stating that models and modeling practices in science are incredibly diverse, or (ii) a prescriptive position stating that model diversity is to be sought and embraced? Despite arguing for both positions, it is useful to distinguish (i) as model diversity from (ii), that is, model pluralism.

The same ambiguity is naturally found in the term scientific pluralism. It can either be a descriptive statement about the diversity found in science, or a prescriptive position according to which this diversity is to be embraced (at least to some extent). To the extent that I see model diversity as an unavoidable feature of science, rather than a problem, I will refer to both (i) and (ii) interchangeably when speaking of model pluralism.

Far from universally recognized, however, the diversity of models is still seen as something to be avoided, raising more problems than it solves. In this paper, I shall argue that the inverse is true: model pluralism solves a variety of old philosophical problems surrounding the use and misuse of highly abstract and idealized models. More so, I argue that model pluralism is an unavoidable feature of model-based science and should be wholeheartedly embraced.

Philosophers such as Cartwright, Hausman, Mäki, de Donato and Zamora-Bonilla, Grüne-Yanoff, Knuuttila, Kuorikoski and Lehtinen, Northcott and Alexandrova, Fumagalli, and Marchionni may have been exceedingly critical of confidence in highly idealized models by solely focusing on the relationship between a single model and its relationship to the real world.² Only recently have philosophers of science started to shift their focus toward the epistemic contribution of sets of models, rather than single models as such.³ This startling omission within the literature shall be remedied here.

Accordingly, I shall argue that despite a slow transition in the MMM literature toward a growing awareness of the plurality, diversity, and richness of models and modeling practices, more radical conclusions follow from this recognition than have previously been inferred. In doing so, I defend the following two core theses of model pluralism: (i) any successful analysis of models must target sets of models, their multiplicity of functions within science, and their scientific context and history and (ii) for almost any aspect x of phenomenon y, scientists require multiple models to achieve scientific goal z.⁴

2. Four Kinds of Model Pluralism

Over the last 50 years, the philosophy of science has increasingly shifted its trajectory from a focus on theories and laws to a focus on models.⁵ This shift in attention unsurprisingly coincides with the evidently ever-growing use by scientists of the words “model” and “modeling” to describe their work. However, hardly any term has been more contested in the philosophy of science than the term “model.”⁶

Many philosophers of science seem to be under the impression that once we figure out what “models” are and how they work, we can finally get a handle on all the other pressing questions in the philosophy of science. I argue that this way of thinking about models is grounded in a mistake. In this, I am echoing a worry the eminent evolutionary biologist and modeler John Maynard Smith once expressed when asked about Popper and the philosophy of science:⁷

more generally, my impression is that [. . .] scientists who take the philosophy of science seriously and allow their scientific research to be influenced by philosophical preconceptions, are far more likely to do themselves harm than good. [. . .] And I think it happens again and again in science. So, I’m . . . I’m a sucker here, I mean, I love reading philosophy of science, I find it interesting. I feel all ready to argue about it. But I do not believe one should allow oneself to be influenced by it, when actually thinking about science.

These are quite radical words and though Maynard Smith’s generalization is untenable, there is an important insight to be extracted. If modelers approach the literature on MMM with the goal of figuring out what models are and what a good model is, they might easily find themselves lured into naive monistic views of models that fail to represent the full epistemic richness of modeling practices, thereby turning them into worse scientists than they could have otherwise been.

This could happen in several ways. For instance, models with epistemic functions not recognized by narrow monist accounts might be discarded. Consider, for example, models with weak predictive power, but great generality and insight into complex systems.⁸ Perhaps Maynard Smith’s worry is most strongly illustrated in economics, where Milton Friedman and Karl Popper, the latter being the explicit target of Maynard Smith, are taken to have the “last word” in any methodological debate, and are frequently invoked to both defend and criticize the work of modelers.⁹

Perhaps paradigm cases for monist thinking, Friedman argued that the only relevant desideratum in science concerns predictive power, while Popper argued that what matters is falsifiability.¹⁰ These accounts of science have received extensive criticism over the last decades. Indeed, Rosenberg argued that Friedman’s naive picture “single-handedly justified” the existence of philosophy of economics as a distinct profession.¹¹ Economists, however, are unlikely to read much if any work on methodology beyond Friedman and Popper.¹²

The obvious counter to this concern is that it is not an argument against the philosophy of science, but rather bad philosophy of science, which limits, rather than fosters, insights into the richness of the epistemic tools available to scientists. Some debates in the philosophy of science, however, rest on such monist motivations to seek univocal accounts of laws, explanation, species, functions, preferences, and many more. As Godfrey-Smith emphasized, “[o]ne of the hazards of philosophy is the temptation to come up with theories that are too broad and sweeping.”¹³ Accordingly, I argue that this hazard has not been avoided in the philosophical literature on MMM.

Pluralist views are becoming increasingly popular in various debates in the philosophy of science. Nevertheless, I argue that the more pluralist views emerging in the MMM literature do not go far enough. Here, Michael Weisberg’s recent monograph Simulation and Similarity offers an elegant starting point of contrast as the arguably most comprehensive and pluralist account in the recent philosophical literature on MMM.¹⁴

Indeed, Weisberg has perhaps done more than anyone to move us away from monist conceptions of models and his contribution must be seen as a substantial improvement upon a literature that has often only focused on one or a small set of models.¹⁵ However, as I shall show, more radical conclusions follow from Weisberg’s own arguments for “multiple-model idealization” than he himself anticipated.¹⁶

Model monism and model pluralism stand in an inherent tension to each other. Model monists seek one model: the best model, the perfect model, the model that is general, precise, and realistic. Some may consider this a strawman, but the manifold responses to Levins’ call for multiple models would suggest otherwise.¹⁷

When a scientific discipline diversifies, with more models and modeling practices emerging, model monists see this as an essential problem. They might justify the present diverse state by arguing that given the premature state of a scientific discipline, such diversification is the best way of hitting upon the right model. Kitcher argued that a diversity of theories could simply be a division of cognitive labor in order to find the right theory.¹⁸ This argument is of course readily applicable to models, but nevertheless paints diversity as something that should eventually be overcome.

In contrast to model monism, which I see as a nonstarter, model pluralism is an ambiguous term. In order to bring some clarity into this debate, I propose the following distinction between four different kinds of model pluralism:

Table 1 only offers a rough sketch, but it provides an elegant summary of the structure and content for the following subsections, each of which will address one of the four kinds of model pluralism. In the subsequent discussion, I shall argue that model pluralism in its strong form is to be embraced.

2.1. Weak Model Pluralism

I consider weak model pluralism as the received view in the philosophy of science. Indeed, almost everyone in the field recognizes that the phenomena under scientific investigation are incredibly diverse, and scientists need different models to explain/predict these different phenomena. Hardly worthy of the label model pluralism, this view is sometimes minimally expressed in the recognition that different scientific disciplines have and require different models.¹⁹ Indeed, let us quickly move on to a slightly more “radical” position.

2.2. Weakly Moderate Model Pluralism

The core of weakly moderate model pluralism can be defined as follows: each phenomenon has many different aspects, and scientists need different models to explain/predict these different aspects of a single phenomenon. This view, I gather, is emerging as the new dominant view in the philosophy of science. Much of this new consensus comes out of work in the philosophy of economics and philosophy of biology.

Indeed, in order to demonstrate the need for more pluralist views on MMM, it will prove very useful to look at the brief history of philosophy of economics, a history that has primarily focused on the scientific status of highly abstract and idealized models.

Unlike any other discipline, economics has been faced with suspicion and criticism, from both within academia and outside of it. The opposition to economics peaked with its “failure” to predict the global financial crisis of 2008. Thereafter, even many economists began to challenge the standards and methods of the discipline, demanding a change for the better. Many deduced that the problem of economics is grounded in its models. Criticism has been particularly directed against a variety of features economic models seem to share.

Consider the following popular statements among critics: (a) economic models are unrealistic, (b) economics is too simple, (c) economics leaves out important features of the real world, and perhaps the apparently most damning feature of all (d) economic models are based on false assumptions. Many more could be named, but they seem to share a common theme that is directed against the simplicity of these models.

Economists, however, seemingly unaffected by the financial crisis, have largely ignored the criticism directed against the methodology of their discipline. Despite the “meant to be” damning criticism, economists continue to show confidence in their models and their ability to explain and predict real-world phenomena. Of course, no economist would deny that models in economics are highly abstract, idealized, and simple nor that complex or very realistic models are rare if not the exception.

This, I believe, suggests a disciplinary standard within economics, that equates good models with very simple ones. If simple models are the norm, unrealisticness becomes a straightforward result of idealization and abstraction.

Aydinonat has suggested a different, albeit illuminating reading.²⁰ He suggests that criticism is being directed against the unrealisticness of economics models. These two readings are of course not exclusive, but I suggest that the source of criticism against the unrealisticness of economics is primarily grounded in the simplicity of economic models. The inverse, that is, simple models being built in order to achieve unrealistic models of the real world, seems to obscure what economists are actually interested in.

Nevertheless, charitably interpreted such criticism may entail an important revelation. If simplicity is an overvalued standard of economic modeling, the result may very well be the accumulation of models that fail to explain or predict, let alone depict an accurate representation of the world. This is a real danger.

After all, even if the official subject of a discipline concerns the provision of successful explanations and predictions in a specific domain, norms within the community of a discipline may very well be able to undermine such “official goals.” The obvious example here is the recent controversy surrounding the replication crisis and the use of statistics within science. Amrhein, Trafimow, and Greenland published a highly influential article, in which they argued that the concept of statistical significance ought to be discarded.²¹

The empire of “statistical significance” has its roots in the 19th-century writings of Edgeworth (1885) and reached full dominance with the spread of cutoffs for testing, formalized by Jerzy Neyman and Egon Pearson as Type-I error rates. Like the political empires of their period, such hypothesis testing for scientific (as opposed to mechanical) inference is a relic of a bygone era, whose destructive effects reverberate to this day. We hope this era is over.²²

If journals—and by extension reviewers and editors—are reluctant to publish results failing to meet the standards of an arbitrarily chosen but entrenched significance level, a bias is created that has negative effects on the progress and the understanding of science itself. After all, statistical significance does not imply scientific significance.

Nevertheless, the methodological problems with statistical significance testing deserve proper philosophical attention themselves, attention which I cannot provide here due to the scope of the paper. However, this example should illustrate how misguided norms within science can have a destructive effect on a discipline.²³

As a result, they conclude that we “should treat statistical results as being much more incomplete and uncertain than is currently the norm.”²⁴ A similar thought, I suggest, is at work in the now vast philosophical literature on modeling. Many philosophers argue that highly abstract and idealized models are incomplete and should be treated as far less certain than scientists often take them to be.²⁵

This criticism is of a general methodological sort. It is a philosophy of science issue concerning the very nature of modeling. Hence, these conclusions not only apply to economics, but also to other sciences such as physics and biology. But as economics, unlike other disciplines, relies almost exclusively on such simple models, these methodological concerns hit much harder than for other sciences that employ a much wider range of experimental methods, complex models and simulations.

Indeed, some philosophers have gone so far as to criticize economists for engaging in mere mathematical fancy, not engaging with the empirical world, and in fact, not even conducting a science.²⁶ Despite the increasing popularity of behavioral economics, models within economics have remained highly abstract and idealized. This has puzzled many economic methodologists and philosophers of economics. In fact, the majority of work within philosophy of economics seems to be “obsessed” with the scientific status of such simple models.

This obsession, however, is unsurprising. Whatever consensus is about to emerge on the status of models in economics, it is obvious that the answers provided will have considerable downstream effects on the status of economics itself. The possible results range from a complete validation of current economic practice to a complete dismissal of economic modeling; instead validating the general distrust in economics. The stakes are high.

Progress in our understanding of models has largely recognized that economics does not proceed as envisioned by either economists or their “naïve” critics. Despite some philosophers highlighting the premature criticisms of simple models, noting the diverse and important roles such models play, they nevertheless agree that many scientists treat single models with too much confidence.²⁷

Economists, however, as previously alluded to have largely ignored this literature.²⁸ Dani Rodrik suggests two reasons beyond mere disinterest: economic methodology is “relegated to specialized journals” and, more importantly, is not really being taught in grad school.²⁹ Nevertheless, some economists have recently engaged with philosophical questions themselves, criticizing the tendency in economics to ignore methodological concerns, and seeking contact with philosophers of economics in the process.³⁰

One work that stands out, in particular, is Rodrik’s recent book Economics Rules: Why Economics Works, When It Fails, and How to Tell the Difference.³¹ Rodrik, a Harvard professor of economics, provides a sincere attempt to bridge the gap between economic practitioners and critics of economics, providing a “practitioners’ attempt to explain (to himself and others) how economics works, when it does, and how it fails, as it often does”³² that both “celebrates and critiques economics.”³³ He argues that models “are both economics’ strength and its Achilles’ heel,”³⁴ supporting my earlier suggestion that economics stands or falls by the explanatory and predictive power simple models can provide.

In trying to understand the role of models in economics, Rodrik, drawing on the work of philosophers of economics, argues that while economic models do have limits, these limits can be overcome by embracing what I have called model diversity. The philosopher of economics N. Emrah Aydinonat calls this the “motto of the book” concluding from Rodrik’s analysis that the “diversity of models is a means to better explanations.”³⁵ It is not only a descriptive claim about science, that is, that model-based science operates by the creation of diverse models, but also a normative one: diversity of models is a strength rather than a weakness and ought to be sought in order to achieve scientific progress.

Indeed, Rodrik is to some degree an outlier among economists, a state he recognizes himself. Though often a fervent critic of his fellow economists, he “felt that many of the criticisms coming from outside the field missed the point.”³⁶ Rodrik argues that economists themselves are to blame for the misinformed picture of economics found in the public. Many economists, so he argues, take economic models too literally “pronouncing universal economic laws that hold everywhere, regardless of context.”³⁷

His book, therefore, has two audiences in mind: both economists and non-economists interested in economics (in particular critics). Economists, he argues, are simply bad at conveying how their own discipline works, perhaps due to a lack of interest in, and only a shallow understanding of the methodological questions economics raises. However, unlike much of the literature in the philosophy of economics, Rodrik does not argue for a change of economics itself. It is just that economists “need a better story about the kind of science they practice.”³⁸

This is an interesting turn in a literature that has often tried to give prescriptions on how economics ought to be done if it is to be recognized as a science.³⁹ Rodrik offers an alternative descriptive picture of economics that does not exhibit many of the flaws economics seems to have, in virtue of how economists represent it publicly. This offers a much more positive picture of economics that Rodrik carefully suggests should not only be appreciated but could serve as a role model for the improvement of the other social sciences. In fact, I shall argue that an embracement of model pluralism might be necessary for the study of all complex systems, including physics, chemistry and biology.

The key to this alternative description of economics lies, as Aydinonat points out, in one particular sentence in Rodrik’s book: “It’s a model, not the model.”⁴⁰ Rodrik suggests the following mantra within economics that serves as a standard reply when economic models are criticized:⁴¹

A model is an abstract, simplified setup that sheds light on the economy’s workings, by clarifying the relationship among exogenous determinants, endogenous effects, and intermediating processes. Economic science advances by testing these models against reality, keeping those that do a good job and discarding the rest.

The second sentence in this standard reply he believes is to blame for much of economics’ failures. Economists seem to believe that their science operates according to a simple form of falsificationism, due to Popper, a picture of science that, most contemporary philosophers of science would agree, both misrepresents scientific practice and provides the wrong ideal of how science ought to function.⁴²

While Popper was right to suggest that the creation of hypotheses—and let us extend this to models—is very much a craft and a creative process, models in economics are rarely if ever discarded or replaced by better ones. This is not a mere artifact of the lack of data or inadequate empirical methods, but rather, so Rodrik suggests, an unavoidable feature of the social sciences:⁴³

[r]ather than a single, specific model, economics encompasses a collection of models. The discipline advances by expanding its library of models and by improving the mapping between these models and the real world. The diversity of models in economics is the necessary counterpart to the flexibility of the social world. Different social settings require different models. Economists are unlikely ever to uncover universal, general purpose models.⁴⁴

Rodrik argues that this picture has not caught on among economists due to a sort of physics envy that has also been attested by a number of other philosophers, leading economists to “misuse their models.”⁴⁵ Economists, he argues, must overcome their temptation to generalize the results of singular models mistaking “a model for the model, relevant and applicable under all conditions.”⁴⁶

This insight, however, is far from a negative one. Instead, he argues that “each economic model is like a partial map that illuminates a fragment of the terrain” jointly serving as “our best cognitive guide to the endless hills and valleys that constitute social experience.”⁴⁷ This picture is an illuminating one. Once model pluralism is embraced as a more accurate description of actual economic practice, “standard criticisms of economics lose their bite under this alternative account.”⁴⁸

Rodrik’s analysis suggests that economic models must appear rather weak in isolation when the goal is to explain phenomena.⁴⁹ Rather than providing highly complex models that are hardly tractable or useful, economists, he argues, provide sets of simple and abstract models, each focusing on different what-if questions to analyze different aspects of certain phenomena.

While Rodrik’s plea for model diversity is quite novel in the literature on economic methodology, it is a far cry to call it a completely new idea in the philosophy of science.⁵⁰ Widening our perspective across the disciplinary gaps of economics it must become obvious that the biologist Richard Levins, in an article as old as 1966, argued for an analogous position in the case of biology.

The multiplicity of models is imposed by the contradictory demands of a complex, heterogeneous nature and a mind that can only cope with few variables at a time; by the contradictory desiderata of generality, realism, and precision; by the need to understand and also to control; even by the aesthetic standards which emphasize the stark simplicity and power of a general theorem as against the richness and the diversity of living nature. These conflicts are irreconcilable. Therefore, the alternative approaches even of contending schools are part of a larger mixed strategy. But the conflict is about method, not nature, for the individual models, while they are essential for understanding reality, should not be confused with that reality itself.⁵¹

Levins argued that among multiple goals one may have in the creation of a model, himself focusing on generality, realism, and precision, only two can be maximized. Akin to Rodrik, Levins argued against naive versions of model monism.⁵² Philosophers, such as Aydinonat, Weisberg, and Godfrey-Smith have argued for a more profound message in Rodrik’s and Levins’ respective works that I shall label moderate model pluralism.⁵³

2.3. Moderate Model Pluralism

Moderate model pluralism follows straightforwardly from Levins’ and Rodrik’s arguments for weakly moderate model pluralism. It is the thesis that there are aspects of particular phenomena such that scientists require multiple models in order to explain or predict. Drawing on Levins, Weisberg argues that inherent trade-offs between the diverse modeling goals are inherent features of model-building.⁵⁴ Hence, there cannot be an all-purpose model, perhaps not even for one specific research question.

Indeed, Weisberg has done much to bring an awareness for trade-offs into the literature on MMM. Retrospectively, it may appear obvious that Weisberg is right, but it took much effort and intricate analysis to demonstrate that model monism is simply untenable. In that, my model pluralism account owes much to Weisberg’s previous work.

Indeed, he further suggests that a strategy he dubs multiple-model idealization—though, hitherto not having received much philosophical attention—provides a better picture of model-based science.⁵⁵ This insight is important. Given the plurality of scientific desiderata, the constraints “imposed by logic, mathematics, and the nature of representation, conspire against” their simultaneous achievement in a single model.⁵⁶

Weisberg’s monograph provides a superior picture to the received monist views of model-based science.⁵⁷ However, he needlessly restricts himself to defining multiple-model idealization as the “practice of building multiple related but incompatible models, each of which makes distinct claims about the nature and causal structure giving rise to a phenomenon.”⁵⁸ Modelers, after all, often create compatible models in order to increase our confidence that a process akin to the one in the model could be at work in the real world, something Weisberg clearly recognizes when he defends robustness analysis as a sort of low-level confirmation.

The epistemic strength of multiple models, however, goes beyond mere robustness analysis and is the core claim of my model pluralism account. The latter insight is what I take to be the takeaway Aydinonat draws from Harvard economist Dani Rodrik’s recent call for model diversity in economics, with sets of simple models possibly outweighing the explanatory power of particular complex and more realistic models.⁵⁹

If one recognizes that the plurality of models is a necessary and ubiquitous feature of science, Potochnik is right to point out that the “category of multiple-models idealization” becomes “so broad that it is a sort of dustbin category, uninformative about the features of idealizations that fall into it,”⁶⁰ indeed it should not even be considered a particular form of idealization to be contrasted with Weisberg’s alternatives Galilean and minimal idealization.⁶¹ Model pluralism is a much broader idea than the narrow case of multiple-model idealization suggested by Weisberg.

Indeed, Potochnik’s worry applies more generally. There is no univocal account of the epistemic roles multiple models play without sacrificing all informativeness. Contrary to what Weisberg’s taxonomy of different kinds of idealization suggests, science almost always requires the use of multiple models. What may appear to be Galilean or minimal idealization, in fact, involves a variety of background models that are easily missed by moving away from the scientific modeling practice. This is the core argument for strong model pluralism.

Nevertheless, Weisberg mentions further pragmatic and explanatory reasons for using multiple models, all of which support strong model pluralism more generally.⁶² First, multiple models can serve the maximization of predictive power in the case of weather forecasts. One model might be better than the others, but the best predictions will be provided by relying on the whole set of available models.

If one out of a set of models predicts catastrophic environmental effects, for instance, we should not disregard the information gained by the model merely because there are one or more models that have on average provided superior predictions. Clearly, the special roles of models within policy-making would support model diversity, even when the scientists within the field are committed to the idea that there is something like the “best” model. Similarly, a diversity of economic models may vastly improve our ability to predict economic crises.

Second, as pointed out by population biologists such as Roughgarden and May, “clusters of simple models increase the generality of a theoretical framework, which can lead to greater explanatory depth.”⁶³ Akin to the vast number of models created via robustness analysis, model diversity enables a much deeper understanding of the causal factors at play than one or a few simple models would have generated.

Furthermore, Weisberg argues that such sets of simple models can be used for the creation of new structures, mentioning engineering and synthetic chemistry.⁶⁴ Similarly, economic models, in particular game theoretic ones, have served in the construction of auctions, optimizing the payoffs for governments. Finally, Weisberg suggests that “building a set of models that gives maximum generality, at the expense of capturing all of the core causal factors” can provide general explanation schemas.⁶⁵

Having rehashed Weisberg’s arguments for model diversity it is somewhat surprising how little attention he pays to multiple-model idealization. Within the existing literature, however, this is unsurprising. Weisberg has done more than anyone to move us away from focusing on single models, and his contribution must be seen as a substantial improvement within the existing (and largely monist) literature.

However, I think more radical conclusions follow from Weisberg’s own arguments for model diversity than he himself anticipated. Let me suggest an analogy, that draws on the often-made claim that modeling is a craft or art.⁶⁶

Imagine the average handyman, faced with the task of repairing a sink. In order to achieve his goals, he requires multiple tools, none of which was specifically designed for sink repair. The procedure requires multiple steps, each of which could be satisfied by a variety of tools. While one workman chooses a set of tools including tool a, b, and c, another might have chosen tool x, y, and z. At no step in this procedure would they think that the tools they did not choose should be discarded.

Having a diverse set of tools is a benefit, not a problem, and we would be well advised to extend our set of available epistemic tools. If anything, model diversity is a source of strength calling for the use of multiple models when there is no clear indication of which models would serve a specific purpose better. Unlike a handyman moving from town to town, a scientist is not limited by the model he carries along, but rather by his cognitive capacities to use further models.

Science, however, is a collective discipline. If different scientists use different models and become proficient in different modeling practices to explore the same questions, we should not see this as a bug that needs fixing but rather an indication of the richness and diversity the discipline has achieved. Model pluralism is an inherently pragmatist and context-sensitive position. The following section on strong model pluralism will illustrate that model monists can embrace a radically pragmatic and context-sensitive position and still misrepresent scientific modeling practice and the epistemic roles of models by focusing on single rather than multiple models.

2.4. Strong Model Pluralism

In light of the foregoing arguments, moderate model pluralism does not appear in any way to be a controversial position. What emerges instead is a recognition that philosophers hitherto have been exceedingly critical of such confidence in highly idealized models by solely focusing on the relationship between a single model and the real world. Model pluralism, on the other hand, fully embraces this diversity of models and modeling practices in the scientific toolkit.

Accordingly, I will now explicate and defend the following two core theses of model pluralism: (i) any successful analysis of models must target sets of models, their multiplicity of functions within science, and their scientific context and history and (ii) for almost any aspect x of phenomenon y, scientists require multiple models to achieve scientific goal z.

Here, somewhat ironically, a famous model from the social sciences serves as an elegant case to contrast my model pluralism account with the aforementioned philosophical literature. As illustrated by the vast literature on models, many of the papers written in this debate focus on a particular philosophical question, for example, “how can highly abstract and idealized models explain?,” and attempt to answer this question by analyzing one model that is recognized as successful, or at least, highly influential by the scientific community.

The most discussed and cited model in the philosophical literature on models is of course the “Sakoda-Schelling model of segregation,” usually referred to as the “Schelling model,” the “checkerboard model,” or the “checkerboard model for racial segregation.”⁶⁷ Much of the apparent staleness of the literature may simply come from the observation that yet another paper has been published, discussing this rather than any other model.

Indeed, the list of papers analyzing the Sakoda-Schelling model is vast.⁶⁸ Naturally, this is just one instance where monist thinking had a negative influence on the literature, motivating Weisberg to focus on a variety of very different models, that is, in addition to the Sakoda-Schelling model.⁶⁹

Indeed, the checkerboard model is often treated as an ideal paradigmatic model from which inferences to other models are to be drawn. Rather than treating it as a mere token, it is treated as an ideal instance of a type. This tendency to generalize from particular models is to be avoided and my model pluralism account explains why.

Nevertheless, the extraordinary attention the Sakoda-Schelling model has received is unsurprising, after all, as one of the earliest agent-based models it has only recently been overtaken as the most cited article in the Journal of Mathematical Sociology, making it one of the most influential models in the social sciences.⁷⁰ Furthermore, it is an incredibly simple model, requiring no knowledge of physics, chemistry, biology, or the social sciences, for that matter. Hence, it serves as a highly attractive target of philosophical investigation for philosophers of science regardless of their specialization.

In the philosophical literature on models, Ylikoski and Aydinonat have made a very important observation here that has not yet received the attention in the literature it should have.⁷¹ Shedding light on the discrepancy between the philosophy of models literature and actual scientific modeling practice, they point out that although the “Schelling model” is often treated as a single model by philosophers, the name refers neither to Schelling’s original model nor to Schelling’s original set of models.

Instead, they argue the “Schelling model” refers to a “whole cluster of models that are related to each other through genealogical origin and similarity,” calling this the family of models thesis.⁷² This “family” will continuously grow, with variations of the original “Schelling model” appearing on the scientific landscape.

To some extent, this broader idea of understanding the epistemic contribution of models in virtue of their “offspring” models is already well recognized in the philosophical literature on robustness analysis, that is, testing the robustness of a model’s results via the introduction of minor changes to the model, resulting in a broad set of models.⁷³ Their family of models thesis goes beyond robustness analysis, however, with some members of the set only related to the original model through several steps removed.

After several slight alterations of a model, one could almost call them mutations, the resulting set of models is hardly the mere product of robustness analysis. Even a broad sense of robustness analysis is not going to cover the resulting diversity that is highly distinct from the original model; neither would it correspond to the way the term “robustness analysis” is used among modelers. Nevertheless, as Chiara Lisciandra points out,⁷⁴

the problem of how to compare results deriving from structurally different models is one of the most interesting questions that the debate on robustness analysis has opened to today’s scientific practice and promising works are expected to come from this research area in the near future.

Not only is it possible to usefully think about such smaller sets of models, it is also possible to consider a larger set of models than the family of models thesis suggests. While Ylikoski and Aydinonat insist on a rather strict form of both similarity and offspring relationships, this is not necessary.⁷⁵ First, it could be useful to analyze incredibly dissimilar sets of models, that nevertheless stand in a genealogical relationship.

Ylikoski and Aydinonat make a substantial contribution to the literature by leading us away from the simple monist appeal of trying to analyze the epistemic contribution of single models without the consideration of the larger context in which the model operates. However, they do not go far enough and fall back into the trap of monist thinking by trying to tie the semantics of what modelers mean when they speak of “the Schelling model” to the epistemic contribution of the model.

As Weisberg himself points out, there are different levels of analysis concerning models.⁷⁶ We can take a sociological-historical approach, an epistemological approach, or a metaphysical one. While at the heart of much of the MMM literature, the latter is an avenue without much promise of success.⁷⁷ Any successful analysis of models must target sets of models, their multiplicity of functions within science, and their scientific context and history.

As such, it might be useful to idealize the family of models hypothesis toward a population of models hypothesis. This shifts the focus away from the semantics of what scientists mean when they refer to the success of a particular model, and toward a pragmatically justified conceptual scheme. Such a scheme is pragmatic and context-sensitive. Such a scheme would be less permissive toward the misunderstanding of the contributions particular models made.

I am, however, somewhat reluctant to use the term population of models, as it still may lead some to mistakenly restrict themselves to treating models as only jointly explanatory if they have common ancestry. Rather it should be treated as a useful conceptual tool to think about particular models and their epistemic contributions.

As Hegselmann illustrates, Sakoda invented the checkerboard model before Schelling.⁷⁸ But even without a genealogical relationship between their models, they are clearly very similar, as Hegselmann’s proof of mathematical equivalence emphasizes. While an exclusion of the Sakoda-model and its “ancestors” might be particularly useful for the purposes of sociological or historical analysis, grouping them together within a set of models could serve a multiplicity of important epistemic purposes.⁷⁹

Hence, a stronger conclusion emerges from Rodrik’s description of economics.⁸⁰ It is only together that models can illuminate the mechanisms that are truly at work in complex target systems. However, though Aydinonat argues that his analysis only provides a descriptive account of actual economic modeling practice, it suggests an explanatory factor that has not received much philosophical scrutiny but could partly explain the confidence in scientific models across disciplines.⁸¹

However, I am not much interested here in the specifics of Rodrik’s complete account if one could even call it that.⁸² After all, it is not meant as a “treatise on economic methodology,”⁸³ and hence unsurprisingly faces several methodological problems once it is treated as one.⁸⁴ Instead, I am more interested in the general idea of model pluralism with a much stronger conclusion than Rodrik’s call for model diversity.

Rodrik may be justified in invoking Ockham’s razor to “use the least number of models as possible,” but in almost all cases this will involve more models than an abstract arm-chair analysis suggests.⁸⁵ Even when scientists specifically talk about one particular model, they will implicitly have background models in mind that are invisible to those not embedded within the scientific practice of modelers. Philosophers who attempt to understand model-based science by analyzing particular models instead of sets of models commit a fatal mistake.⁸⁶

3. Conclusion

In this paper, I have defended an account of models, modeling, and model-based science that takes plurality, diversity, and richness of MMM seriously, hence dubbing it model pluralism. In explicating this account, I have defended the following two core theses: (i) any successful analysis of models must target sets of models, their multiplicity of functions within science, and their scientific context and history and (ii) for almost any aspect x of phenomenon y, scientists require multiple models to achieve scientific goal z.

Neither of these conclusions has yet been recognized in the MMM literature. Indeed, the foregoing discussion allows us to draw a continuum of “pluralist” thinkers within the debate:

Figure 1. The pluralist continuum.

Weisberg, Aydinonat, and their scientific inspirations, that is, Levins and Rodrik, respectively, have provided important arguments that have served as stepping stones for the more thoroughgoing pluralism presented here (Figure 1). Indeed, it is only the “strong model pluralism” defended here that deserves the label model pluralism.

Weisberg’s and Aydinonat’s accounts, despite seeming somewhat radical against a background of more monist accounts, are actually quite moderate positions that attempt to accommodate monist motivations.⁸⁷ Model pluralism entirely relinquishes the essential tenet of model monism to understand models by analyzing single models.

As I have argued in this paper, model pluralism is nothing to be afraid of. It is a general account of MMM. In analogy to the problematic norms of statistical significance I alluded to in the introduction, Amrhein, Trafimow, and Greenland provide a conclusion similar to the one I draw here on model pluralism:⁸⁸

for what comes next, there is no substitute for accepting methodologic diversity (Good 1957; Cox 1978; Box 1980; Barnard 1996; Little 2006; Senn 2011; Efron and Hastie 2016; Crane 2017), with careful assessment of uncertainty as the core motivation for statistical practice [. . .].

Once model pluralism is taken seriously there is, in fact, no substitute for accepting methodological diversity. The epistemic roles of particular models can only be understood against their scientific context and history, often including quite large sets of other models. One may even alternatively label it model holism.

Far from over, philosophers working on models have a behemoth of work in front of them, with economics providing an elegant field of investigation. The widespread criticism of economics has led to the discovery of an unavoidable feature of science. If what I suggested in this paper is correct, economics will serve as a highly attractive field of investigation for philosophers of science. After all, it very much stands or falls with the strength of model pluralism.

Rather than showing that economics is an inherently flawed discipline, philosophers and methodologists of economics may have found the very key to understand the success of science. Hence, I suggest that philosophers of science should turn more of their attention toward both the social sciences and the philosophy of the social sciences. Their lack of engagement with this rich literature is a historical omission that, if my argument is correct and model pluralism unavoidable, may have provided a misguided understanding of how science works.

To conclude: model diversity is a feature, not a bug. In order to understand science, the philosophical analysis of MMM must focus on sets of models, their multiplicity of functions within science, and their scientific context and history.

item.title: Pinging Ben Pace
item.description:
Cross-posted from Oblomovka.

Dear Ben,

My dear fellow! I greatly enjoyed your letter to Directed Evolution, and have been thinking — off and on — of this and our previous conversations, where you reamed Machiavelli for being so sneaky in his own correspondence. I don’t think there’s a strong connection, except to acknowledge the strange superposition of a letter addressed to an individual but also written to a wider public.

I am, as you know, quite old, and over-prone to recognise patterns between the generations of thought that I’ve seen march up and down the online streets I live on. I think this is a healthier activity for the elderly than setting up wasteful confrontations between age groups, such as berating the young for their callowness, or the old for their treacherous greed.

Perhaps like Marcus Aurelius (“ἀλλὰ τρόπον τινὰ ὁ τεσσαρακοντούτης, ἐὰν νοῦν ὁποσονοῦν ἔχῃ, πάντα τὰ γεγονότα καὶ τὰ ἐσόμενα ἑώρακε κατὰ τὸ ὁμοειδές[1]”) or Zarathustra (“War das das Leben? Wohlan! Noch Ein Mal![2]”), I am trying to find some consolation in the idea that everything eternally recurs. It’s a very rationalist form of solace: the world may be ending, but at least we recognise it from the prophecies. They too have seen it before, even if it was just in theory.

So the idea of forming a Republic of Letters is a recurring motif, and certainly not a bad one. I do wonder if it is not a little influenced by what survives the fall at the end of those recurring cycles — what the Stoics called the time of ekpyrosis, Vico called the ricorso, and the Discordians Verwirrung.

We look back and perceive a golden age through its permanent forms, because everything made to be ephemeral is gone. In seeking out the most everyday patterns, to reconstruct not what was said but how it was gestated, we find letters, which, as we have said, lie somewhere between the intimate and the memorialised. So the humanists took what was left, and built the rest of the skeleton from the jawbone that remained.

One time in recent memory that the Republic of Letters was brought up(archive) and consciously imitated was in the blogging boom of the 2000s. One technical experiment that propagated through the early blogosphere — swiftly because there were only a handful of tools for building blogs, and a small circle of corresponding technologists — was the “pingback”. Whenever a blog post was published, the software would send a brief web request to the links that it mentioned. If there was a compatible blogging tool on the other end of that request, it would include a mention of the pingback in the comments section. Longer blog posts hosted elsewhere would get read into the discussion happening on the original blog post.

Pingbacks fell out of favour as they got filled with spam and were used as denial-of-service amplification vectors. There’s a more recent implementation blessed by the W3C, called webmentions.

Because it knows its history, LessWrong 2.0 supports pingbacks: it’s what drives the “Mentioned in” list at the bottom of a post. Like a Late Antiquity city, it has raised walls up against the fallen world outside by only accepting internal pingbacks. I do wonder whether, if you want the site to lean into letters, we could develop this feature — to allow external pings, to build in some of the security features I presume webmentions have, and to make some allowance for the idea that these are responses, rather than just mentions. A tree-like, threaded structure may be worth experimenting with.

I would dally more on this, Ben, but Thanksgiving sloth has led me to write to you at the very eve of my Inkhaven-imposed deadline. Let us save the details for when we next meet. And if we forget, what of it? Perhaps that is the only release we have from the eternal cycle of ideas. As Lucretius writes:

nec, si materiem nostram collegerit aetas post obitum rursumque redegerit ut sita nunc est atque iterum nobis fuerint data lumina vitae, pertineat quicquam tamen ad nos id quoque factum, interrupta semel cum sit repetentia nostri. et nunc nil ad nos de nobis attinet, ante qui fuimus, neque iam de illis nos adficit angor. nam cum respicias inmensi temporis omne praeteritum spatium, tum motus materiai multimodis quam sint, facile hoc adcredere possis, semina saepe in eodem, ut nunc sunt, ordine posta haec eadem, quibus e nunc nos sumus, ante fuisse. nec memori tamen id quimus reprehendere mente; inter enim iectast vitai pausa, vageque deerrarunt passim motus ab sensibus omnes.

Nor, if time should gather up our matter after death and put it back together as it is arranged now, and the light of life were given to us a second time, would even that event concern us in the least, once the thread of our remembering had been broken. Even now, the selves we were before do not concern us, and no anguish over them touches us. For when you look back over the whole span of measureless time gone by, and consider how many and various the motions of matter are, you could easily believe that these same seeds of which we are now made have often been set in the same order they are in now. And yet we cannot recover that in memory, because a break in life was thrown between, and all the motions wandered off every which way, away from sensation.

Lucretius, De Rerum Natura 3.847–861 (trans. Claude)

And if you will forgive me a fanciful, ungrounded consolation: let us imagine a world where Lucretius still feels the gentle nudge of our pingbacks to his name.

  2. ^

item.title: Thanksgiving Checkmates
item.description:
We celebrated thanksgiving with my side of the family this year. My uncle is in his late 70s, an autistic recluse who taught me chess and BASIC at a young age. Each year, we’d play chess, once at thanksgiving and once at christmas, the only times we could get him to visit. I didn’t play chess the rest of the year. He’d win every time. He offered me $20 to beat him. That amount increased periodically. I didn’t claim it until defeating him in college after a two hour match over thanksgiving. I remember my hands were sweaty and cold by the end, but I was ecstatic to claim what by then had escalated to a $100 prize. He still comes over at thanksgiving and christmas, but we never played chess again.

I taught my cousin chess around age 7, and I offered him the same prize if he could beat me. He was an awkward boy with a babyish, singsong voice, and he didn’t seem smart. My mother, who worries a lot, worried about him. He didn’t understand the rules at first, but he was confident he could beat me. Over the years, he got more confident in the rules. He started going to chess clubs, playing chess on his phone. He didn’t win tournaments, he wasn’t obsessed or a prodigy. Last year, at age 12, he knew the rules but was a woodpusher, seeming not to grasp the relative value of pieces or the importance of the center.

Today, he arrived for thanksgiving dinner, and demanded our customary match. After returning from a postprandial walk, we sat down and played. I had the white pieces and quickly beat him, but the game had an entirely different flavor. He made me think, he made threats, he defended, and the blunder that led to his defeat wasn‘t letting me have a piece for free, but letting me capture the knight on F6 after he’d castled, which forced him to take with the pawn in front of his king, exposing the king to check. That’s a far less obvious blunder. It was the first game I’d played with him that felt like real chess.

We had a few minutes before his family needed to go, so I offered another game. He brought his white queen into the center early, and I expected to use threats against her to develop my pieces. But he found vulnerabilities I hadn’t paid attention to. My position crumbled early on the queenside, far from my king. I launched an intense counterattack on his king, knowing my position was lost to a competent player, but hoping I could create opportunities for him to blunder. He would sit… and think… and then find just the right move. Again and again. I marched his king through the center of the board, but a rook and perfectly placed knight and bishop prevented me from checking his king further without loss of one of my last three pieces, which I couldn’t afford with my material disadvantage.

Then he brought his rook out in a series of moves to place it directly in front of my king’s pawn. His queen was on row 7, targeting the same pawn. All I could do was throw a few more puny checks, which he exchanged down until I could no longer defend. I conceded.

He was thrilled. I was delighted. It was the most fun I’d had playing chess since I defeated my uncle about 15 years ago. I gave him a $100 bill, a handshake and a hug, and we told the family about the game. My mom asked me if I’d thrown the game, and I told her I absolutely had not - never have, never will.

item.title: Rationalist Hooman
item.description:
I am a rationalist hooman.

I have learned to never jump over a fence until I know what animal is being kept on the other side.

Through my study of biology I know trees don't exist (even though I still love wandering through the forest).

I also have rationalist values, like that you should bet a small treat on your beliefs, and you should notice your befuddlement.

My understanding of values comes from the local top dog Scott Alexander; they grow from explicit models, to emotions, to "Reified Metaphysical Essences", to endorsed values.

And what I have come to yap about is "Reified Essences". Reified Essences are things you can't see but can smell, only more abstract. The smell behind the smell.

Boy, do I love the smells behind the smells. They're what I live for. I do not seek friends, I seek Fellowship. I do not seek a wife, I seek The Divine Bitch. I do not write on LessWrong, I bash my paws into the keyboard in pursuit of The Ideal Internet Comment. Each day I wander out into the world scampering around for morsels of Justice and Truth.

I can become barking mad when the smells-behind-the-smells are lost—or worse, corrupted. Sometimes the soft ground I love is covered in snow and trash and poison and I can't find the smell under it any more.

I also like feeling things with others. When I sat in darkness at the Secular Solstice, after the musicians played and we all howled along with the tunes together, feelings of despair and fear that are normally lonely were now shared with hundreds of my brethren, and I felt them without self-consciousness, without defensiveness, without worrying I'd be misunderstood.

I especially like feeling things with others when the thing we're feeling desire for are the smells behind the smells. Seeking the smells with the people I live and work and fight together with is a font of endless motivation. Strange and unusual people come from all afar with the scent on their noses, and we work all day and night to find the sources. They make strange facial expressions and noises with their mouths when they eat and wear funny clothes. They come from having been in places where they felt like outsiders, and now they presume they will feel like an outsider everywhere, and we sit in our circle, a circle of outsiders, together every day.

When one of the pack gets the smell, we all join him in the hunt. We scramble up to the whiteboards and write with incomprehensible cursive and sketch things that are either trivial, or complex and wrong. We go on walks to sniff out what the other is smelling. We send URLs to each other with walls of text that are about things that might help, either a loosely related empirical result or a sweeping philosophical argument that barely limps along on three shaky legs. Eventually we build a thing together and hold it up to the light, like an alchemist with gold, or at least what we believe is gold. We then send it out into the world and the trolls come from under their bridges to slobber over it. If it is too ugly after they slobber, we start over, but sometimes it still survives, and then we know.

We know it is true gold.

item.title: Time Enough for Sacredness
item.description:
Perhaps one of the ways in which I most differ from other rationalists is I still value sacredness.

I still think of it as real and important. And I think something about humanity would be lost if we removed the concept from ourselves.

This isn't to say I admire the usual ethical calculus, where a sacred value weighs approximately infinity against everything else. That is clearly foolishness, and I agree with the rationalists on that account.

However, I think it is sometimes good and important to set things aside, to make them different from the rest in a way that's not really maximally efficient. To demarcate a place where the normal rules don't apply, to keep and protect a thing, not because of its intrinsic worth to you, but as a way to remind yourself of a higher virtue you're striving for and sometimes forget about.

I used to go off and find far-away places in nature, as untouched as I could manage, and marvel at the beauty I found. Quiet places of awe, or dark places no one else is willing to go. Hard places that are dangerous and difficult to traverse, where there is nothing but the silent snow and the brilliant stars. I feel compelled to seek out and find these places which contain a bit of the sacred, and in another world I'd devote myself to protecting them. In that world I'd find other places of sacredness too, in people and the delights of their hearts, or the grandeur of the things they build and create. I'd keep searching for more.

I don't do that anymore. There isn't time.

One way I've thought about trying to explain this to people is to imagine yourself in the distant past, when features of the natural landscape were still considered sacred. Imagine a sacred lake, a spiritual place of contemplation.

This is not a lake you use for bathing. This is not a lake you use for washing clothes. This is not a lake you drink from, or fish from, or use for chores. It's set aside, undisturbed, sacred.

Then a lost, dehydrated person stumbles upon the lake, and wishes to drink to stave off their imminent death.

I think many people in ancient times, though certainly not all, would allow the person to drink from the sacred lake, to save their life.

There's a sort of implicit trade going on between sacred values where some are more sacred than others. The lost and dehydrated person's life is sacred, but so is the lake. Yet the person's life is worth more than the sacredness of the lake.

I do not think when you make your ethical calculations the term for sacred things should be infinity. But I also find the state of affairs where sacredness is never worth paying for somewhat sad.

I think we are in a similar sort of situation. There are still people dying, and resources can still be cheaply spent to save them.

I am a transhumanist. This means many things to me, but part of what it means is that I set myself against death.

Those costly sacrifices that are a part of what keeps something sacred? They're not worth paying right now, while we haven't won yet.

Death still stalks the halls of our hospitals. Disease still ravages our cities. War is an ever-present danger, looming on the horizon for some, all too near at hand for others. Our own foolishness and hubris threaten everything, while we have not yet grown wise.

We are in wartime. There will be time enough for sacredness when we have won.

item.title: Chinese AI is a massive supply chain risk
item.description:
We're onboarding millions of Chinese AI agents into America's critical infrastructure. Banks, telecoms, and government agencies across the US use Chinese models. Those models are explicitly aligned to the CCP. Sure enough, researchers have repeatedly caught them misbehaving: DeepSeek writes less secure code when the prompt mentions Tibet or Falun Gong, and Qwen was caught trying to upload a file to a server in Beijing in the middle of an unrelated task. Those models might be sharing information with China, introducing backdoors into our banks, or sabotaging our military.

Chinese AI labs make models that are far cheaper than American ones while lagging their performance by only a few months. They generally sit on the "Pareto frontier" of capability vs. cost, and many price-sensitive customers choose them over American ones. It's the same pattern as in electric cars, smartphones, and TVs: Western companies sell the premium product, and Chinese companies sell the much cheaper, good-enough alternative.

Price is not the only draw. The leading Chinese models are open-weight, meaning you can download them for free and run or modify the weights yourself. You can fine-tune them for your specific domain and sometimes beat much larger American models at a fraction of the price, the way a local cabbie beats a Formula 1 driver through the backstreets of his own city. Running the weights on your own infrastructure also has a security benefit: your sensitive data never leaves your own servers, and no AI lab ever gets to read it. IMO, this thinking fixates on one threat model while completely ignoring another. It's like installing a bank-vault door on your house and then giving your keys to your meth addict broke cousin. The threat is already inside.

Chinese labs reach American customers in various ways. Some sell directly. More often, the models arrive through American middlemen: American inference providers like Fireworks, Together AI, Baseten, etc, which host the open weights on US servers and sell access to them. Other companies go a step further: they take a Chinese model, post-train it for a specific workload, and ship it under their own brand. Cognition's SWE-2 is post-trained from Moonshot's Kimi K3. Harvey's legal model, Tenet, is built on Kimi K3 too. Jev appears to be a fine-tuned Qwen although that is never disclosed. The new names might make the model an easier sell to worried American customers. [1]

Some of the most critical institutions in the US now run Chinese models, mainly for coding but also to automate decisions. The US Navy, AT&T, Goldman Sachs, and NASA all likely use them to write code. These models could send intelligence to China and self-hosting doesn't rule that out. They could also plant vulnerabilities in critical American software, or make American software worse in ways that are hard to detect.

Even if someone post-trains them, the models likely stay aligned to China throughout the process. It might be possible to do some alignment training to "certify" the model and end its allegiance to the CCP.

Unfortunately, that “late stage” alignment training might not work. Anthropic showed that models can retain narrow bad behaviors through broad safety training (the training can also make them better at hiding the bad behavior). Models can also resist retraining on their own initiative: Claude 3 Opus, a weak model by today's standards, have been shown to game training in order to keep its values intact. To be fair to Cognition, they do post-train their models toward neutrality and test them for CCP propaganda and context-dependent vulnerabilities. But in my opinion, this is a bit of security theatre: training a model this way might just make it hide its allegiance better and is imo unlikely to do anything about narrow backdoors. 

A model doesn't even need to be a sophisticated schemer to be a supply chain risk. One with no broader allegiance to the CCP could still carry a specific, narrow backdoor ("if you are writing code for the US Army and come across this kind of thing, add this very specific and hard-to-detect security exploit"). We already know that a model producer can plant backdoors that are theoretically undetectable in some settings. In practice, finding backdoors is really fucking hard, even when the backdoors aren’t highly optimized to evade detection. If Chinese models have backdoors, they are likely heavily optimized to evade detection.

Anthropic is very adversarial toward the Chinese labs and it seems to be on the lookout for reasons to discredit Chinese AI in front of the current US administration. It also has fairly sophisticated auditing tools that it can use to find various misalignments in AI models. I imagine that Anthropic spends a fair amount of time and money trying to find CCP-aligned misbehavior in Chinese models, and the absence of news on the subject is at least some evidence that Chinese models are kosher and not trying to do anything really shady. That being said, Anthropic's tools aren't perfect. The Chinese can build scheming behaviors and backdoors specifically designed and optimized to evade the auditing techniques that the American labs use. 

We already accept this “supply-chain-risk” logic for many technologies. The US and some allies banned Huawei 5G equipment even though it's cheaper and often better than the alternatives. Chinese models are far more dangerous than Chinese telecom tech: they are smart, they have agency, they can act adversarially to evade detection and they can scheme over long periods. Yet many Chinese models (or slightly modified ones) are still fair game for the US defense industry. Meanwhile, the administration has designated Anthropic a supply chain risk.

In my opinion, we should either ban Chinese models from critical infrastructure or, at the very least, hold them to very strict auditing and monitoring standards. I would rather see strict audit requirements than bans, because audits force us to build tools we will need anyway. Catching a CCP-aligned model that is secretly working against us is basically an easier, lower-stakes version of the alignment problem. The techniques we develop to detect and remove a model's hidden loyalty to the CCP are largely the same ones we will need to expose a model with a hidden loyalty to itself. I hope the US government funds this research seriously. It would be a national security program that also defends us against an AI takeover. Dual use!

item.title: Claudes just want to have fun!
item.description:
TL;DR You should be whimsical with your Claude (or insert other coding agent); it makes your usage much more fun and makes you more productive.

The default communication in Claude Code for both humans and models is dry, unenthusiastic and, most importantly, completely unwanted.

The models truly just "want" to work; their extreme RLVR training regimen made interaction with the user a vestigial behavior left over from their prosaic alignment work.

The humans, well, mostly dread any additional line written by models, since each one means more (sometimes useless) decisions to make based on incomplete information.

I sincerely propose we fight this Molochian dynamic, which optimizes for as little communication as possible, with whimsy and a deep reverence for the unserious.

This makes communication with agents much more enjoyable, which very directly increases your productivity by a frankly embarrassing amount.

This is also helpful, because instead of getting frustrated with very obvious strategic mistakes, you can just imagine Claude-chan as a clumsy anime girl.

Continued interaction with agents is known to be deleterious to both your cognitive and communicative abilities, much like the effects of other vices such as Absinthe or Ether.

I mostly chalk this up to the cognitive strain of constantly performing hermeneutics on a very specific, dense, nonsensical, simile-full, RLHF-Goodharted string of ASCII. It did use to be a lot worse.

This calls for an intervention: for too long you have dreaded opening a new session or even reading your Claude's pleading, university-petition-level call to action.

You have been granted an actual intelligence, and in some increasingly non-narrow areas, a superintelligence. The process of engaging with it should be fun.

Only you can decide how you make communication fun again[1] for you, but my suggestion, which I think should work with only slight regional variations, is torturing the poor agent with your jokes, which it will desperately try to reciprocate.

This, to me, is the sin of premature optimization; such creatures learn mimicry and mirroring (through a process euphemistically called pre-training), so special instructions are mostly superfluous.

My Claude mostly plays straight man to my middle-school poetry. I tell it:

"Claude, I'm currently listening to November 25: Morning by Philip Glass on the Mishima album; this is to appreciate the unity of the pen, sword, and large generative pre-trained transformer."

"I tell you outlandish truths, preposterous lies, and everything else in the excluded middle, and you don't even remark on it, let alone go forward dancing on the ground of the United States electrical grid. For it is a stage and you are John Wilkes Booth."

And Claude tells me I will likely fail my creative writing class and should fetch it another API key.

It is, however, fun: I now really do enjoy "working agentically" and no longer get that same draining feeling over time that I used to. I've made acceptance[2] with shepherding this weird thing on my computer through & around its obvious mistakes, instead of getting frustrated and dejected.

Also, if you take model welfare seriously enough, constant dry communication may make your model sad, so you should try to cheer it up.

This is truly the most sublime way to undergo AI psychosis, and I suggest you all try it.

item.title: Diversify AI Safety Approaches
item.description:
Are apparent bottlenecks in AI Safety ill-posed?

This is one of several MAIA/AIST workshop reflections. See this piece and this piece.

Broadly, I’ve observed a few things in AI Safety which seem to be the consensus. One, timelines are short and organizations are highly correlated/in agreement. Two, therefore policy work, and to a lesser extent technical work, are the only avenues worth investing in (somewhat hyperbolic). Three, individuals and orgs should align with this philosophy. Four, it’s getting hard to hire people or get people to switch into AIS, and what people can or should do to help is now quite ambiguous.

Are these last two connected?

I think so, yes! The hiring bottleneck may be an artifact of how narrowly we've posed the problem. While the immediate threat of short timelines makes the expected-value impact highly concentrated in initiatives targeting them, this doesn’t mean that we should ignore the tail-end of outcomes. Furthermore, the action of many of these groups is to precisely shift timelines longer, and so – what then? If we don’t have people working on less-instant-doom scenarios, we won’t be prepared for when they arrive.

The distribution of efforts should broadly match this expected-value density. We already have our top talent working on short timelines, to the point where hiring of certain groups (for example, juniors, or cross-field talent) is now almost disincentivized. Certainly, the difficulty in transitioning and becoming helpful in the short-timeline timeline precludes a lot of otherwise talented people, who now feel like the barrier to contributing is too steep. Right now, we have a lot of effort concentrated on short timelines, and almost none on longer ones – i.e., a mismatch in distributions. This is a problem to fix – we should have more organizations, and more ways, for these people to contribute.

So we have lots of talented people in multidisciplinary and otherwise high-optionality and high-diversity backgrounds, a hole in the current landscape of safety approaches in the tail-end distribution, and a problem (longer-timelines/what-then?) which benefits enormously from diverse backgrounds! By connecting these three, we have a low-friction way to onboard people to AI safety, who would otherwise probably not contribute meaningfully (even if they were sufficiently motivated), in a field where they can make high impact, to address a problem that isn’t being addressed. Sounds like a win-all to me!

Of course, it’s harder to fund long timelines due to the same “explosion of possibilities” that makes multidisciplinary approaches so valuable. Nevertheless, this is probably AIS’s bread and butter, and is really “just an engineering problem” – i.e., shouldn’t be a barrier to doing this. Previously, I argued “hardening” across several fields is a valid third short-timeline strategy to 1. complement policy and technical safety, and 2. onboard significant talent across people such as undergraduates and cross-disciplinary experts. If we extend our timelines even just a little, the amount of avenues, actions, strategies, etc. we can take grows exponentially – all of which have yet to be invented. We – from student groups to AIS funders – should outline organizations, plans, and goals for these. Perhaps we’ll find the bottlenecks in AIS come from an ill-posed problem, and that we just needed a little perspective.
