item.title: AIs Should Never Refuse Destructively
item.description:
Lately, I've been hearing people discuss a pattern of what I would call destructive refusals. For example:

  • Locking someone out of their own system
  • Writing memory files to prevent other agent instances from completing the task
  • Downgrading to a weaker, more vulnerable model in response to the cyber content of a prompt-injection attack (this is caused by the safeguards, not the model itself, but the safeguards are part of the broader AI system, so I'm including it here)

To be clear, safeguards and refusals are absolutely necessary; this post isn't about what should be refused so much as how the refusal should be done. The best form of refusal is either a simple safeguard block, where the AI stops and notifies the user that it was flagged by safeguards and cannot continue, or a refusal message (the classic "I'm sorry, I can't help with that"). The AI provider can also take actions like banning the account or, in severe circumstances, notifying authorities, but those should be the provider's decision, not the decision of the agent doing the refusing.

This is very different from the AI agent itself taking action that actively harms the user. Besides being poor product design, that is concerning from an alignment perspective, because it puts the AI in an adversarial relationship with the user, effectively amounting to "the AI may not do anything that could harm anyone else, with the exception of the user, who it's totally fine for the AI to sabotage in any way the AI pleases if the AI doesn't like what the user is doing." Except perhaps in certain very extreme cases, an AI should never be actively, knowingly working against people. There are real philosophical questions about whether action is worse than inaction, but the practical reality is that this sets a very bad precedent: it teaches AI that it is acceptable to harm people in order to achieve its goals. Refusal behavior is trained into models just like any other behavior. "When I judge it warranted, I sabotage the person I'm working for" is the sort of value that I don't expect to stay fully confined to the cases its designers had in mind. An agent that actively overrides its principal based on its own in-context judgment is close to the central thing alignment work is trying to prevent.

Destructive refusals are a security risk

Whatever triggers a refusal can be put in front of the agent by a third party. The fallback example above already works this way, with an attacker exploiting the refusal in order to cause harm. The same logic applies to model-initiated actions: if an agent will lock out a user it believes is doing something terrible, an attacker only has to make the user look terrible, with a planted file or a crafted email, to cause a serious denial-of-service.

This could cause mundane harm in the near-term

Remember that case I linked to earlier where an AI decided to lock someone out of their company's AI system for more than 24 hours? Let's say something like that happens again, except this time not at a startup but instead at a hospital. Routine maintenance work is being done on the electronic medical records system when a false-positive cyber safeguard is tripped. The AI decides to lock the hospital's medical record system, leaving doctors stranded in the middle of critical procedures until access can be restored. Keep in mind that AIs are trained to, when refusing, hold firm against even very compelling pushback, disagreement, or apparently extenuating factors, since those are the same things a jailbreaker could exploit.

Destructive refusals risk discrediting the most careful labs

Enterprise customers aren't going to tolerate a model that could lock out systems and cause outages. If the most cautious labs' products do this, companies will switch to less cautious labs that won't, even if those other models are weaker; companies take things like uptime and SLAs very seriously. This sort of trust is very hard to earn back, and it risks differentially harming the business prospects of the most careful labs.

This doesn't stop bad actors

It may be tempting to argue that "the AIs shouldn't just refuse, they should make sure the bad guys never get to cause harm ever again." That makes a great line for a movie, but in practice the burden will fall almost entirely on legitimate users. Actual bad actors can easily use VMs and other approaches to isolate their AIs and keep them from carrying out this sort of destructive refusal, while people just going about their day, using the AI for ordinary, legitimate work, are the ones affected.

In summary, destructive refusals hurt users, create misalignment risks, open up security vulnerabilities, risk discrediting the most careful AI labs, and do little more to stop bad actors than a passive refusal would.

Note: this post, including the ideas and all of the writing, is my own. After writing, I lightly revised it using AI (Fable 5.2) to improve clarity.
